title: Potential Energy in Mechanics
short_intro: Potential energy is the mechanical energy stored within a system due to the spatial configuration or relative positions of its interacting bodies under conservative forces. It is defined mathematically through the negative line integral of a conservative force field.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of potential energy, work-energy relation for conservative forces, gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface (U = mgh), elastic potential energy of a spring (U = &frac{1}{2}kx²), and conservation of mechanical energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General conservative force fields, derivation of force from potential (F = -∇U), central force potentials, gravitational potential due to mass distributions, stability analysis of equilibrium using potential energy curves (d²U/dx² > 0), and potential energy in non-inertial frames.

prerequisites: Work, power, and kinetic energy theorem
Line integrals and vector calculus basics
Newton's laws of motion and conservative forces

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Conservative Force Field
bullets: Potential energy U is defined only for conservative forces where work done is independent of the path taken.
The change in potential energy ΔU between two points is equal to the negative of the work done by the conservative force: ΔU = -W = -∫<sub>A</sub><sup>B</sup> F · dr.
The dimension of potential energy is [ML²T&sup-;²] and its SI unit is the joule (J).

concept_notes.heading: Relation Between Force and Potential Energy
bullets: In one dimension, the conservative force is related to potential energy by F(x) = -&frac{dU}{dx}.
In three dimensions, force is the negative gradient of the potential energy scalar field: F = -∇U = -(&frac{partial U}{partial x}i + \frac{partial U}{partial y}j + \frac{partial U}{partial z}k).
The negative sign indicates that the force always acts in the direction of decreasing potential energy.

concept_notes.heading: Mechanical Energy Conservation
bullets: The total mechanical energy E = K + U of a system remains constant if only conservative internal forces do work.
Any increase in kinetic energy corresponds to an equal decrease in potential energy and vice versa.
Non-conservative forces like friction dissipate mechanical energy into thermal energy, violating simple mechanical energy conservation.

concept_notes.heading: Equilibrium and Potential Energy Curves
bullets: Stable equilibrium occurs at local minima of potential energy, where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² > 0.
Unstable equilibrium occurs at local maxima of potential energy, where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² < 0.
Neutral equilibrium occurs where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² = 0 over a finite displacement region.

derivations.title: Gravitational Potential Energy Near Earth's Surface
derivations.conditions: Uniform gravitational field (g is constant), vertical displacement y.
steps: Write the gravitational force acting on a mass m pointing downward: F = -mg j.
Express the change in potential energy using the line integral: ΔU = -∫<sub>y<sub>1</sub></sub><sup>y<sub>2</sub></sup> F<sub>y</sub> dy.
Setting U = 0 at reference level y<sub>1</sub> = 0, the potential energy at height h is U(h) = mgh.

derivations.title: Elastic Potential Energy of a Linear Spring
derivations.conditions: Spring obeys Hooke's Law, displacement x from natural length.
steps: Write the restoring force exerted by the spring: F<sub>s</sub> = -kx, where k is the spring constant.
Use the work-potential energy relation: dU = -F<sub>s</sub> dx = -(-kx) dx = kx dx.
Integrate from equilibrium position (x = 0) to extension x: U(x) = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>x</sup> kx' dx'.
Perform the integration to obtain the stored elastic potential energy.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential Energy Well and Phase Interpretation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve of U(x) versus x showing a smooth bowl-like minimum, with horizontal total energy line E intersecting the curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The region where E > U represents allowed motion where kinetic energy is positive. The turning points occur where E = U. The minimum represents stable equilibrium.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: To determine turning points of motion, particle velocity at various positions, and stability analysis.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force Determination from U-x Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An arbitrary non-linear potential energy curve U(x) with tangent lines drawn at various points.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The force at any point is the negative slope (-dU/dx) of the tangent at that point. Steeper slopes indicate larger magnitudes of force.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct qualitative and quantitative questions asking for the direction and relative magnitude of force from a given U-x graph.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Verification of Hooke's Law and Elastic PE
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of restoring force vs displacement (straight line passing through origin) and work done (area under the curve representing U).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed under the F-x graph up to extension x equals the potential energy stored in the spring (&frac{1}{2}kx²).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: TGT/PGT conceptual questions linking graphical integration to stored energy.

solved_numericals.question: A body of mass 2 kg is lifted vertically upwards through a height of 5 m. Calculate the change in its gravitational potential energy. (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
solution_steps: Identify given values: m = 2 kg, h = 5 m, g = 9.8 m/s².
Apply the formula for gravitational potential energy: ΔU = mgh.

solved_numericals.question: The potential energy of a particle of mass 1 kg moving in one dimension is given by U(x) = 8x² - 4x³ Joules. Determine the position of stable equilibrium and the angular frequency of small oscillations about this equilibrium point.
solution_steps: Find the first derivative of U(x) with respect to x: dU/dx = 16x - 12x².
Set dU/dx = 0 for equilibrium: 4x(4 - 3x) = 0, giving x = 0 and x = 4/3 m.
Test stability at x = 0: d²U/dx² = 16 > 0 (Stable equilibrium).
Test stability at x = 4/3: d²U/dx² = 16 - 24(4/3) = 16 - 32 = -16 < 0 (Unstable equilibrium).
Calculate angular frequency at stable equilibrium (x = 0): ω = √(k/m) where k = d²U/dx² = 16 N/m. Thus ω = √(16 / 1) = 4 rad/s.
solved_numericals.answer: Stable equilibrium at x = 0; Angular frequency ω = 4 rad/s

solved_numericals.question: A conservative force field is given by F = (2xy + z³) i + x² j + 3xz² k. Find the potential energy function U(x, y, z), assuming U = 0 at the origin (0, 0, 0).
solution_steps: Use the relation F = -∇U, which gives &partial;U/&partial;x = -(2xy + z³), &partial;U/&partial;y = -x², and &partial;U/&partial;z = -3xz².
Integrate &partial;U/&partial;x with respect to x: U(x,y,z) = -∫ (2xy + z³) dx = -x²y - xz³ + f(y, z).

Differentiate this intermediate U with respect to y and equate to -&partial;U/&partial;y (-x²): -x² + &partial;f/&partial;y = -x² &implies; &partial;f/&partial;y = 0, so f depends only on z: f(y,z) = g(z).
Differentiate U = -x²y - xz³ + g(z) with respect to z and equate to -3xz²: -3xz² + g'(z) = -3xz² &implies; g'(z) = 0 &implies; g(z) = C (constant).
Using the boundary condition U(0,0,0) = 0, find that C = 0.

assumptions_and_limitations: Potential energy is strictly defined only for conservative forces; dissipative forces like friction cannot be represented by a potential energy function.
The absolute value of potential energy is arbitrary and depends on the choice of the reference zero level; only potential energy differences have physical significance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Potential energy is an intrinsic property of a single isolated object.
common_misconceptions.correct: Potential energy is a property of a system of two or more interacting bodies interacting via a conservative force.
common_misconceptions.why: Gravitational or elastic potential energy depends on the relative separation between the object and the Earth or spring respectively.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A negative potential energy means the particle is bound and cannot move.
common_misconceptions.correct: Negative potential energy simply reflects the choice of setting U = 0 at infinity; particles with negative total mechanical energy are bound, but they can still move between turning points.
common_misconceptions.why: Zero potential energy is a matter of convention; kinetic energy can still be positive.

quick_revision: Potential energy is defined via change in energy as ΔU = -W<sub>conservative</sub>.
Force is the negative spatial derivative of potential energy: F = -dU/dx.
Stable equilibrium corresponds to a local minimum of potential energy (dU/dx = 0, d²U/dx² > 0).
